newsitem.title: USA: Foreign angle dominates campaign finance hearings.
newsitem.headline: Foreign angle dominates campaign finance hearings.

text.p: Republicans used the third day of Senate hearings on alleged campaign finance abuses on Thursday to suggest that the Democrats were lax in protecting against possible foreign donations and influence.

The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee grilled Richard Sullivan, the Democratic National Committee's (DNC) former finance director, for more than five hours about the mechanics of the Democrats' 1996 fund-raising effort.

Several Republicans zeroed in on the role of John Huang, a former DNC official who prospected for donations from the Asian-American community, raising $1.6 million that has since been returned because it was deemed questionable.

They also queried Sullivan, appearing for his second day of testimony, about fund-raising events that brought President Bill Clinton into contact with foreign citizens and about the DNC's safeguards against improper foreign donations.
Democrats on the committee, which began its hearings on fund raising in the 1996 presidential election on Tuesday, argued their party's practices largely mirrored those of the Republicans.

Sen. John Glenn of Ohio, the committee's ranking Democrat, told reporters after the hearing that there had been talk of much damaging material emerging from Sullivan's testimony but added, "I didn't see that happen."

In one new disclosure, Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine told the hearings that Democratic Party donor Yogesh Gandhi last year received cash transfers from a Japanese bank and suggested these may have covered his donations.
Collins said Gandhi gave the DNC $325,000 at a May 1996 dinner. The DNC later returned the money, saying it could not verify its source.
While questioning Sullivan, she said that in August 1996 Gandhi testified in court he had no funds in the United States and insufficent income to file U.S. income taxes.

"Would it surprise you to know ... committee investigators have uncovered a wire transfer from a Japanese bank for this amount into Mr. Gandhi's personal account?" Collins asked. "Is this yet another example of the DNC failing to do a sufficient job to screen a very large contribution that's coming in from a source that's never contributed before?"

The committee released copies of bank transfers to Gandhi worth $250,000 each on May 20 and May 23, 1996, originating from a person or entity only as "Yoshio Tanaka." Under U.S. law, foreigners and foreign companies are generally barred from making political contributions.

There are exceptions for foreigners who are legal U.S. residents, like Gandhi, or for the subsidiaries of foreign companies that have substantial U.S. operations and could have covered their donations from the subsidiaries' U.S. income.

Collins also said Gandhi had been rebuffed by the White House when he sought a meeting with Clinton but that after he made the $325,000 donation the DNC arranged for him to meet Clinton at the May 1996 dinner.

The DNC said last November it had returned the donation from Gandhi, who claims to be a distant relative of Mahatma Gandhi. At the time, the DNC said he gave Clinton a life-sized bust of the Indian spiritual leader at the dinner.

The hearings have focused on whether foreign countries sought to sway the U.S. political process by targeted campaign donations. Sen. Fred Thompson, the Tennessee Republican chairing the panel, opened the hearings by saying he believed China plotted to influence U.S. politics and foreign policy.
The committee, which concluded its questioning of Sullivan on Thursday, is scheduled to resume its hearings on Tuesday.
